strengths: Addresses critical gap in interpretability of vision-language models with a comprehensive, systematic approach to extracting spatially-grounded, hierarchical concepts

Exceptionally thorough experimental validation including large-scale user study (1000+ questions, 5 annotators), quantitative metrics, and multiple downstream task evaluations across classification, segmentation, captioning, and open-vocabulary segmentation
Technical approach well-motivated and clearly presented with rigorous mathematical formulations; novel combination of SAEs, concept hierarchy discovery, and hierarchy-aware naming
Achieves competitive performance on standard benchmarks while enabling interpretability, demonstrating practical utility without significant performance trade-offs
Excellent presentation with comprehensive appendices, detailed training procedures, and extensive supplementary results supporting reproducibility
Discovers meaningful semantic concept hierarchies that align with human understanding, providing valuable insights into learned representations
weaknesses: Concept naming quality remains imperfect with some concepts receiving overly general names; hierarchy-aware naming only partially addresses this fundamental limitation, and impact on downstream tasks is not fully analyzed
Computational cost and scalability not addressed: training requires 2B samples, inference overhead compared to baselines unknown, and applicability to larger modern foundation models unclear

Limited analysis of failure modes and cases where the method breaks down; predominantly shows successful examples without quantifying failure rates or characterizing which concept types are problematic
Novel evaluation metrics, while comprehensive, are not yet standard in the field; consistency metric heavily relies on annotation quality with incomplete inter-annotator agreement characterization
Design choices inadequately justified: hierarchy threshold τ=0.75 lacks justification, optimal Matryoshka SAE structure not theoretically motivated, choice of K=12 only empirically validated
Limited direct comparison with related interpretability methods (CLIP-Dissect, CBMs); distinctions from concurrent concept-based approaches not clearly articulated
Potential bias propagation through CLIP embeddings used for concept naming; no analysis of whether discovered hierarchies reflect demographic or cultural biases; limited ethical impact discussion
Multiple-parent DAG hierarchy structure could create ambiguous relationships but trade-offs between tree and DAG representations not analyzed

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: interpretability of vision-language models with spatially-grounded concepts
Comprehensive experimental validation including quantitative metrics, large-scale user study (1000+ MTurk questions), and multi-task evaluation across classification, captioning, and OVS
Enables interpretable downstream task predictions with steering capabilities, not limited to classification
Thorough documentation with extensive appendices providing training details, ablations, and qualitative examples
Clear visualizations of concept hierarchies, spatial groundings, and application examples
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: sparse autoencoders for concept extraction are well-established; hierarchy discovery uses simple co-occurrence thresholding (Eq. 2) without principled threshold selection; concept naming relies heavily on existing CLIP embeddings and templates

Questionable evaluation methodology: automated GPT-5-mini judge lacks validation against human agreement; user study with minimal context may not reliably assess concept quality; co-occurrence statistics used to claim semantic hierarchies without validation that discovered structures are meaningful

Hierarchy Discovery Issues: purely statistical discovery from co-occurrence (not semantic analysis); no comparison to hand-crafted or established taxonomies; threshold selection admits to being 'qualitative' rather than principled

Weak downstream task performance: classification results (78.9 vs 78.3 SALF-CBM) show CFM is competitive but not superior; some baselines match or exceed performance; no discussion of interpretability-performance tradeoffs or clear practical advantages

Scalability and generalization concerns: evaluated only on CLIP-DINOiser; fixed design choices (8192 concepts, K=12) not validated; no computational cost analysis; unclear applicability to other vision models
Naming accuracy still limited: only ~32% BERT-based improvement (Fig. 5); fine-grained concepts explicitly acknowledged as having limited naming capability; vocabulary constrained by CLIP

Limited comparison to alternative interpretability approaches: focuses on concept bottleneck models and SAE variants; missing comparisons to attention visualization, prototype networks, and other vision-language interpretability methods

Reproducibility issues: no mention of code release; complex vocabulary construction with multiple filtering stages; many hyperparameter choices appear empirically tuned without justification (e.g., Matryoshka ratios, α=1.33)
Insufficient failure analysis: no principled method to identify 'bad' concepts; some hierarchical relationships appear questionable (Fig. C4); no cross-dataset generalization evaluation

strengths: Addresses a critical and timely problem: making language-aligned vision foundation models interpretable through hierarchical concepts—highly relevant for trustworthy AI and vision-language research
Comprehensive and well-integrated technical approach combining SAEs, Matryoshka hierarchies, co-occurrence analysis, and hierarchy-aware naming in a principled manner

Exceptionally thorough experimental validation including quantitative metrics (locality, consistency, purity, impurity), large-scale human study (~1000 questions across 3 tasks with rigorous design), and multi-task evaluation (classification, captioning, open-vocabulary segmentation)

Strong empirical results: competitive classification performance while providing the only interpretable explanations; demonstrates practical utility for decision steering and interventions; user study confirms concepts are more consistent and meaningful than baselines

Excellent presentation with clear figures (especially Figs. 1-2, 4), logical flow, and comprehensive 30+ page appendices covering metrics, user study design, training details, and hyperparameter ablations
Demonstrates practical applicability beyond interpretability research with concept-level interventions for image captioning and steering capability for segmentation tasks
Honest discussion of limitations (concept naming challenges, vocabulary constraints) and acknowledgment of areas for future improvement
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: while the integration is novel, individual components (SAEs, Matryoshka SAEs, co-occurrence analysis) are established techniques from prior work; main contribution is their thoughtful combination rather than new methods
Computational efficiency not addressed: missing analysis of SAE training time, inference latency, memory requirements, and scalability to larger models—critical factors for practical adoption

Incomplete failure case analysis: while limitations are mentioned, deeper investigation of when hierarchies break down or concept naming fails is limited; examples like 'electricity' and 'solar panel' showing no visual coherence deserve more analysis
Concept naming remains imperfect (~20% error rate in Figure 5) and inherently limited by CLIP's vocabulary; fine-grained concepts may inherit overly general parent names

Human study rigor could be improved: uses crowdsourcing with potentially variable quality, inter-annotator agreement not reported for relationship rating task, and full annotator training protocols not detailed
Limited theoretical justification: why co-occurrence signals hierarchy is assumed but not formally justified; threshold τ=0.75 appears dataset-dependent without sensitivity analysis
Evaluation metrics are relatively simple (locality, consistency, impurity); could benefit from information-theoretic measures or more sophisticated grounding metrics
Minimal societal impact discussion: inherited biases from CLIP not addressed; potential misuse of concept-based explanations and concept fairness not analyzed
Limited generalization analysis: evaluation primarily on CLIP ViT-B/16; cross-model and cross-domain transferability to other foundation models (DINO, medical imaging, etc.) not explored

Incomplete related work coverage: recent concept-based explanation methods and vision-language model interpretability literature could be more extensively reviewed; comparison to feature visualization methods lacking
